title: What AI at Work Can and Cannot Do
body:
AI tools at work are good at certain jobs and poor at others, and a worker who knows the difference uses them well while a worker who does not gets misled. AI is strong at drafting, summarizing long documents, reformatting text, finding patterns in large sets of records, and producing first drafts of routine material. It is weak at knowing whether a fact is true, at judging a situation it has never seen, at handling confidential or sensitive material safely, and at taking responsibility for a decision. A useful rule is that AI proposes and humans dispose: the tool can prepare material, but a person must check it, own it, and answer for it before it leaves the team.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part capability check done before any work task is handed to an AI tool. First, name the task in one sentence and ask whether it is a language or pattern task, which suits AI, or a judgment, fact, or responsibility task, which does not. Second, ask what would go wrong if the output were plausible but wrong, and who would notice. Third, decide in advance how the output will be checked and by whom, using the companion Verifying AI Outputs Database for the checking method itself. Fourth, keep a human as the named owner of the final result, so no task ends with nobody responsible for it.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for what ai at work can and cannot do. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: draft a memo -> suits AI; summarize a report -> suits AI; approve a payment -> needs a human; judge a grievance -> needs a human; tasks needing a human: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when starting to use an AI tool for real work, when a team is unsure which tasks suit AI, or when an AI result has already caused confusion. Do not use it as a promise that any particular tool is safe for a particular task, because tools differ and change, and the check must be repeated for each new tool and each new kind of task. Do not use it to hand a consequential decision to a tool, because no AI output carries accountability. title: AI Limits and Failure Modes at Work
body:
AI tools fail in ways that look like success, which is what makes them risky at work. An AI can invent a quotation, a date, or a reference that reads perfectly but does not exist. It can state an uncertain claim with full confidence, mix two different cases into one answer, or follow the wording of a question so closely that it confirms a false premise instead of correcting it. It can also go stale, answering from training that predates a rule change, a price change, or a new policy. A worker who expects these failure modes treats every AI answer as a draft to be checked, while a worker who does not may forward a confident error to a customer, a manager, or a record that will be trusted later.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-item failure watchlist kept beside any AI-assisted task. First, invented specifics: names, numbers, dates, and references are the most likely inventions, so they are checked first. Second, false confidence: a smooth, certain tone is not evidence, so certainty in the answer is ignored as a signal. Third, premise errors: if the question assumed something wrong, the answer may build on it, so the premise is checked separately. Fourth, staleness: any claim about a current rule, price, or policy is checked against a current source. Fifth, mixed cases: where two similar cases exist, the answer is checked to see which one it actually describes.

Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record to train workers before they rely on AI output, and as a refresher after any AI-caused error at work. Do not use it as a complete checking method: the step-by-step method for checking claims, sources, numbers, and citations lives in the companion Verifying AI Outputs Database, and this record deliberately does not duplicate it. title: Why AI Output Needs a Human Check
body:
Every AI output at work needs a human check, not because AI is useless but because its errors are hard to spot. A human writer who is unsure hedges, pauses, or says so; an AI tool usually writes smoothly through uncertainty, so the reader gets no warning. That smoothness is the danger: a manager reading a fluent summary, a customer reading a confident reply, or a colleague copying a neat table will all assume the material was verified, when in fact nobody has verified it yet. The human check is the step that turns an AI draft into a work product, and the person who checks it becomes its owner. Without that step, errors travel further and faster than they ever could from a single human mistake, because AI makes errors at machine speed and scale.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-part attitude, not a checklist, and it stays deliberately at that level so it does not duplicate the companion checking method. First, treat every AI output as an unverified draft, whatever its tone. Second, decide before acting whether the output will be used, and if so, route it through the checking method in the companion Verifying AI Outputs Database, which carries the steps for claims, sources, numbers, citations, and media. Third, never forward, file, or publish AI output that has not passed that check, and say plainly when material is AI-assisted so the next reader knows its status. The demo below simply counts how many items in a small batch are still unchecked, which is the number that matters before anything is sent.

title: Automation and Your Role
body:
Automation changes roles more often than it removes them outright, and workers who understand that pattern adapt better than workers who expect either safety or doom. A typical automation story runs in three stages: first, a tool takes over the most repetitive part of a job, such as copying data between systems; second, the worker's time shifts toward the parts the tool cannot do, such as judging exceptions, talking to people, and fixing what the tool gets wrong; third, the job itself is redefined around supervising, checking, and improving the automated process. Some roles shrink and some disappear, and that risk is real, but the most common outcome is a changed role, not an empty desk, and the workers who fare best are those who learn the supervising and exception-handling parts early.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-question role review that any worker can run about their own job. First, which parts of my week are repetitive, rule-based, and already partly automated, and which parts need judgment, conversation, or physical presence? Second, which of the automated parts do I currently check, and what would I need to learn to check them well? Third, which exception cases land on my desk when automation fails, and am I the person who knows how to handle them? Fourth, what skill would make me the person who improves the automated process rather than the person it replaces? The answers sketch a personal direction: toward supervision, exception handling, and process improvement.

Do not use it as a guarantee about any particular job, because automation effects differ sharply by task, sector, and employer, and no general record can promise an outcome for one role. Do not use it to dismiss workers' worries, because worry about a changed role is reasonable and deserves a concrete plan, not reassurance alone. title: Workplace AI Privacy Basics
body:
Privacy at work changes when AI tools enter the picture, because what a worker types into an AI tool may not stay inside the workplace. Some AI tools keep prompts, some use them to improve the service, and some pass them through systems the employer cannot control, which means a worker who pastes a customer record, a salary discussion, a medical note, or an unreleased plan into a public AI tool may have disclosed it outside the organization. The rule that protects workers is simple to state and easy to forget under deadline pressure: treat anything typed into an AI tool as shared outside the team unless the employer has said in writing that the tool is approved and contained. When in doubt, leave the sensitive detail out and ask how the tool handles data before using it for real work.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part privacy screen applied before any work material goes into an AI tool. First, sort the material: public, internal, or sensitive, where sensitive means personal data, customer data, commercial secrets, or anything that would cause harm if disclosed. Second, check whether the tool is employer-approved and what its data handling says about retention and reuse, in plain terms, not marketing terms. Third, remove or replace sensitive details before prompting, using placeholders instead of real names, numbers, and cases. Fourth, never paste credentials, keys, or private identifiers into any AI tool. Fifth, if the tool's handling is unclear, do not use it for that material, and ask the employer for a written answer.

title: Human Oversight: Staying in Charge
body:
Human oversight means a named person stays in charge of AI-assisted work from start to finish, and it is what separates using a tool from being used by one. Oversight has three parts: the human decides what the tool is asked to do, the human checks what it produces before it is acted on, and the human can stop, change, or overrule the tool at any point. Oversight fails in a familiar way called automation bias, where people stop checking because the tool has usually been right, and then miss the one case where it is wrong. Good oversight is therefore designed, not assumed: checking duties are assigned, time is allowed for them, and overruling the tool is treated as good work, not as slowing the team down.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part oversight assignment for any AI-assisted workflow. First, name the human owner for each step: who asks, who checks, and who approves. Second, set the check that fits the stakes: a quick read for a draft, a full check for anything sent outside the team, and a second person for consequential decisions. Third, keep a stop rule: any checker who is unsure stops the workflow and escalates, without needing permission to pause. Fourth, record the decision and its checker, so the chain of responsibility is visible later. The demo below shows a workflow where one step lacks an owner, which is the oversight gap to fix before the workflow runs.

Do not use it to spread responsibility so thinly that nobody owns anything, because oversight shared by everyone is oversight held by nobody. title: AI Policy at Work: Reading the Rules
body:
Most workplaces now have an AI policy, and most workers have never read it, which leaves them guessing about rules that already answer their questions. A typical workplace AI policy covers five things: which tools are approved and which are not, what data may and may not be entered, whether AI output must be disclosed and how, who is responsible for checking AI-assisted work, and what happens when the policy is broken. Reading the policy with those five questions in mind turns a long document into a short personal rulebook: my approved tools, my data limits, my disclosure duty, my checking duty, and my escalation route. Workers who cannot find a policy should ask for one, because working without written rules means every worker invents their own, and inconsistent invention is where breaches happen.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-question policy read-through. First, list the approved tools and note whether the tool you actually use is on the list. Second, extract the data rules into a personal shortlist of material you must never enter. Third, note the disclosure rule: when must AI assistance be declared, and in what form? Fourth, note the checking and ownership rules: who checks, and who answers if the output is wrong? Fifth, note the escalation route: who do you ask when a case falls outside the policy, and what do you do while waiting? Write the answers on one page and keep it where you work, because a policy you cannot consult at the moment of use is a policy that will not be followed.

Do not use it to justify using an unapproved tool because it seems better, because approval exists precisely to control data and risk, and the remedy is to request approval, not to proceed quietly. title: AI, Bias, and Fair Treatment at Work
body:
AI tools can treat people unfairly at work, not out of intent but out of pattern: a tool trained on past decisions repeats past patterns, including patterns that disadvantaged some groups, and it does so consistently and at scale. At work this matters in hiring screens, performance summaries, shift allocation, customer handling, and any ranking or sorting of people. The worker-facing lesson is not to build fairer models, which is a specialist job, but to recognize the warning signs: a tool that systematically rates one group lower, a summary that turns a single incident into a character judgment, or a recommendation that nobody can explain. When a worker spots such a pattern, the right response is to pause, preserve the evidence, and escalate through the employer's fairness or grievance route, not to quietly correct individual cases while the pattern continues.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part fairness watch. First, compare outcomes across groups where the data allows it, looking for systematic gaps rather than single cases. Second, ask whether the tool's reasons can be explained in plain language, and treat an unexplainable recommendation about a person as a reason for human review, not as a verdict. Third, check whether the input data itself is skewed, for example a performance history that reflects who got the good assignments rather than who did good work. Fourth, keep the human decision separate from the tool's suggestion: the tool advises, the human decides, and the human can explain the decision without hiding behind the tool.

Use and limits. Use this record for anyone whose work involves AI-assisted judgments about people, and in training for hiring, management, and customer-facing roles. Do not use it as legal advice about discrimination law, which differs by jurisdiction and turns on specific facts; this record is educational reference only. title: Data You Should Not Put Into AI Tools
body:
Some work material should never go into an AI tool, and the list is worth memorizing because deadline pressure makes it easy to forget. Never enter credentials, access keys, or private identifiers. Never enter another person's personal data, such as health details, salary, disciplinary history, or private contact information, into a tool that is not approved for that data. Never enter unreleased commercial material, such as pricing plans, merger discussions, or source code the employer has not cleared for outside tools. Never enter material covered by a confidentiality agreement or by professional secrecy, such as legal or medical case material. The test is simple: if disclosing the material outside the organization would cause harm, embarrassment, or a breach of trust, it does not belong in an unapproved AI tool, and if the tool's approval is unclear, it does not belong there either.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-second screen run before every prompt that contains work material. First, scan the prompt for names, numbers, identifiers, and case details, and replace each with a placeholder or remove it. Second, ask whether the prompt contains anything from the never-enter list, and if it does, stop and use an approved channel instead. Third, after the answer arrives, check whether the answer itself reveals anything sensitive, because an AI can repeat or infer details from a prompt in ways the user did not intend. Teams can practice this screen with sample prompts until it becomes habit, because a habit survives deadline pressure better than a rule remembered only in training.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for data you should not put into ai tools. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. title: Automation, Skills, and Reskilling Paths
body:
When automation changes a role, the useful question is not whether to learn something new but what to learn, in what order, and with what evidence that it matters. Reskilling paths that work share a shape: they start from the worker's existing strengths, add one supervising or exception-handling skill that the automated process actually needs, and prove it with a small real task rather than a certificate alone. A data-entry worker who learns to check automated entries, investigate exceptions, and explain errors to customers has a path; a worker sent to a generic course with no link to their team's new workflow does not. Employers, training providers, and workers all have a part: the employer names the new skills the team needs, the provider teaches them in work-shaped tasks, and the worker chooses the path that fits their strengths and their life.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-step reskilling plan. First, map the current role into tasks and mark which are automated, which are changing, and which are new. Second, pick one target skill from the changing or new column, choosing the one the team needs most and the worker can build on fastest. Third, learn it through a real task: shadow the person who does it now, take on a small supervised version, and collect evidence that it worked. Fourth, review after a fixed period, such as six weeks, and either deepen the skill or pick the next one, so the plan stays a loop rather than a one-time course. The demo below counts a small skill plan by status, which is the review a worker and manager can do together.

Do not use it to push all reskilling onto the worker, because employers who automate a process owe their teams a realistic path through the change, including time and support to learn. title: Talking to Managers About AI Changes
body:
Workers often need to raise AI concerns with a manager: a tool that keeps erring, a workflow that no longer allows proper checking, a privacy worry, or a role change nobody has explained. These conversations go better when they are framed as work problems with evidence, not as resistance to change. A useful structure is to name the specific case, show the effect on the work, name the risk if it continues, and propose a concrete fix, such as a checking step, a different tool approval, or a short training session. Managers respond better to one clear case and one fix than to a general complaint about AI, and workers protect themselves by keeping the conversation in writing, such as a short email summary after a verbal discussion, so agreements are not lost.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part conversation plan. First, pick one concrete case: the date, the tool, the output, and what went wrong or what worried you. Second, describe the work effect: delayed work, a customer impact, a risk to a record, or time lost to rework. Third, propose one fix that is within the manager's power, such as adding a checking step, pausing use for one task type, or requesting a policy clarification. Fourth, agree the next step and the date to review it, and confirm it in writing. If the concern involves safety, privacy, or fair treatment and the manager does not act, the worker should use the employer's formal reporting route, and keep their own dated notes of what was raised and when.

Use and limits. Use this record before raising an AI concern at work, and in manager training on receiving such concerns. Do not use it as legal advice about whistleblowing or employment rights, which differ by jurisdiction; this record is educational reference only. Do not use it to avoid raising a serious concern, because a concern about safety, privacy, or fairness that is never raised cannot be fixed, and the formal route exists for exactly those cases. title: Designing a Team AI Oversight Routine
body:
A team AI oversight routine is the weekly or per-project rhythm that keeps AI-assisted work checked, owned, and improving, and it is the most practical form of literacy for a team that already uses AI tools daily. The routine has four beats: a short check of what AI-assisted work is in flight and who owns each piece, a review of errors or near-misses found since the last routine, a decision about any tool or policy change needed, and a note of what the team learned, kept where new joiners can read it. The routine works because it is small and regular: a fifteen-minute review that actually happens beats a grand governance document that nobody opens. Its product is not paperwork but a team that catches its own errors earlier each month.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step routine design. First, fix the rhythm: weekly for busy teams, per-project for slower ones, and never longer than a month between reviews. Second, fix the attendees: the people who actually check AI work, not only managers. Third, fix the inputs: the list of AI-assisted outputs since last time, the errors found, and any policy or tool questions raised. Fourth, fix the outputs: named fixes with owners and dates, plus a one-paragraph learning note. Fifth, fix the escalation: which findings go to management, to the policy owner, or to the formal reporting route, and by when. The demo below shows a routine agenda where one item lacks an owner, which is the routine's first fix.

title: Automation Risk Assessment for a Work Process
body:
Before a work process is automated, a worker-facing risk assessment asks what could go wrong, who would be harmed, and what would catch it, in plain language rather than technical jargon. The assessment covers five risks: wrong outputs reaching customers or records, sensitive data leaking through the tool, workers losing the skill to do the task by hand when automation fails, unfair treatment of some people by the automated step, and loss of accountability when nobody can explain a decision the system made. Each risk is rated by how likely it is and how serious it would be, and each gets a countermeasure: a check, a limit, a fallback, or a decision not to automate that step. A process where a serious risk has no countermeasure is not ready to automate, whatever its promised savings.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-row assessment table built by the people who actually do the work, not only by the people buying the tool. First, list the process steps and mark which ones the automation would touch. Second, for each touched step, name the worst plausible failure and who it would affect. Third, rate likelihood and seriousness in simple terms: low, medium, or high. Fourth, assign a countermeasure and an owner for each medium or high risk, choosing from checking, limiting, fallback to manual work, or excluding the step from automation. Fifth, set a review date, because risks change as the tool, the data, and the team change. The demo below scores three risks and flags the one that is both likely and serious, which is the first to fix.

Use and limits. Use this record before automating a process, when an automated process starts erring, and in team discussions about new tools. Do not use it as a formal compliance assessment, because regulated sectors have their own assessment duties, and this record is educational reference only. Do not use it to approve automation on the strength of a low average risk, because one high-seriousness risk without a countermeasure outweighs several low ones. title: AI at Work: Rights, Records, and Recourse
body:
Workers have practical rights and routes when AI affects their work, and knowing them in advance matters more than discovering them during a dispute. The exact rights differ by jurisdiction, but the useful pattern is consistent: workers can usually ask what tools are used on their work, what data about them is processed, and how an AI-assisted decision about them was reached; they can usually ask for a human review of a consequential decision; and they can usually raise concerns through internal routes, worker representatives, or regulators where those exist. Records matter here: a worker who keeps dated notes of what tool was used, what it produced, what was checked, and what was raised, and when, is in a far stronger position than one relying on memory. This record explains the pattern so workers know what to ask and what to keep, not so they can act as their own lawyers.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part personal file kept by the worker. First, a tool note: which AI tools touch your work, and what the employer's policy says about each. Second, a decision note: any AI-assisted decision about you, what it said, and what explanation was given. Third, a concern note: any worry raised, to whom, on what date, and what response came back. Fourth, a recourse note: the internal route, the worker representative, and the external route that applies in your jurisdiction, written down before they are needed. Keep the file outside any system the employer alone controls, in a form you can still reach if you change roles, and keep it factual: dates, quotes, and documents, not characterizations of people's motives.

Use and limits. Use this record in worker training, union and representative briefings, and personal planning. Do not use it as legal advice: employment and data rights differ by jurisdiction and by contract, and anyone facing a real dispute should seek qualified advice promptly. Do not use it to collect other people's private data, because a personal file about your own work is legitimate record-keeping, while gathering colleagues' data is not. title: Workplace AI and Confidentiality Agreements
body:
Confidentiality agreements and professional duties do not pause when an AI tool is convenient, and workers sign or accept them in many forms: employment contracts, client agreements, non-disclosure agreements, and sector codes for fields such as law, health, and finance. The core promise is the same in each: material entrusted to you stays within the circle the agreement names, and using an outside AI tool can break that circle even when nothing is published, because the material has still left the circle. The worker-facing test is therefore not whether the AI answer was useful but whether the input was permitted to leave: if the agreement, the policy, or the client instruction does not clearly permit outside processing, the safe course is to keep the material inside approved systems and to ask for written permission before using an outside tool on it.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-question confidentiality check run before AI use on restricted material. First, what agreement or duty covers this material, and who is inside its circle? Second, does the employer's AI policy name this tool as approved for this class of material, in writing? Third, does the tool's data handling keep the material inside the circle, or does it retain, reuse, or route it elsewhere? Fourth, if any answer is unclear, what approved alternative exists, such as an internal tool, a redacted version, or manual work, and who can give the permission needed? A check that cannot be completed is itself an answer: do not proceed until it can be, and record the question and the answer given, so the next worker does not have to ask again.

Do not use it as legal advice about any specific agreement, which must be read in full and, where the stakes are high, reviewed by a qualified adviser; this record is educational reference only. title: A Worker's AI Literacy Plan
body:
A worker's AI literacy plan is a personal, one-page plan that turns general advice into dated steps: what you will learn, in what order, and how you will know it worked. The plan has five lines: the tools you actually use and the policy rules for each, the failure modes you will watch for, the privacy screen you will run before prompting, the checking route you will use through the companion verifying-ai-outputs pair, and the skill you will build next as automation changes your role. A plan written this way is useful because it is personal: it names your tools, your tasks, and your next skill, rather than repeating generic guidance. It is also reviewable: after a month, the worker and their manager can see which lines held, which failed, and what to change, which is how literacy becomes a habit rather than a course attended once.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-line plan built in one sitting and reviewed monthly. First, list your tools and the policy rule for each in one line per tool. Second, write your personal failure watchlist: the two failure modes most likely in your tasks. Third, write your privacy screen as three reminders you will actually run before prompting. Fourth, name your checking route: the companion database's method, plus the person who checks consequential work with you. Fifth, name one next skill tied to automation in your role, with a date to start and a small real task to prove it. The demo below tracks a small plan by status, which is the monthly review in miniature: lines done, lines in progress, and lines not started are all visible at a glance.
